pos: v. (brought under; conquered and held; Hebrew kabash, kana')
etymology: Latin subdere, to put under. The Hebrew kabash is the word of Genesis 1:28 — subdue the earth — and it means to bring under and keep under, not merely to defeat.
biblical_def: Subdued is the language of a conquest completed and held. Moses lays the condition on Reuben and Gad before they may settle east of Jordan: “And the land be subdued before the LORD: then afterward ye shall return, and be guiltless before the LORD, and before Israel; and this land shall be your possession before the LORD” (Num 32:22), repeated to them in the same terms (Num 32:29). The siege law uses it of a city: “thou shalt build bulwarks against the city that maketh war with thee, until it be subdued” (Deu 20:20). Joshua reaches the moment: “And the whole congregation of the children of Israel assembled together at Shiloh, and set up the tabernacle of the congregation there. And the land was subdued before them” (Josh 18:1). And the judges' formula uses it of an oppressor put down: “So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. And the land had rest fourscore years” (Jdg 3:30). Note where the tabernacle goes in Joshua 18. The land is subdued, and the first thing set up on it is the house of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subdue as to conquer by force and bring into permanent subjection; to reduce under dominion; to overcome by discipline; to soften.
webster_full: SUBDUE, v.t. To conquer by force or the exertion of superior power, and bring into permanent subjection; to reduce under dominion.
2. To oppose successfully; to overpower; as, to subdue the passions.
3. To destroy the force of; to overcome; as, to subdue the temper.
4. To soften; to make less harsh or severe.
scriptures: And the land be subdued before the LORD: then afterward ye shall return, and be guiltless before the LORD, and before Israel; and this land shall be your possession before the LORD.
Only the trees which thou knowest that they be not trees for meat, thou shalt destroy and cut them down; and thou shalt build bulwarks against the city that maketh war with thee, until it be subdued.
Josh 18:1
And the whole congregation of the children of Israel assembled together at Shiloh, and set up the tabernacle of the congregation there. And the land was subdued before them.
Jdg 3:30
So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. And the land had rest fourscore years.
corruption_summary: Dominion is either abandoned as domineering or seized as licence to exploit, while Genesis and Joshua make subduing a stewardship exercised before the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase Moses uses is the governing one: the land be subdued before the LORD. Not before Israel, not for Israel — before the LORD. The same verb appears in the creation mandate, where man is told to subdue the earth, and the qualifier is the same in principle: dominion is exercised by a creature under a Creator. Strip the qualifier and you get exploitation; strip the mandate and you get the modern instinct that any human ordering of creation is presumption. Scripture gives both halves and keeps them together.

Joshua 18:1 shows what subduing was for. The land was subdued, and the congregation assembled at Shiloh and set up the tabernacle. The conquest was not an end; it was the clearing of ground for worship. A church that conquers anything — a habit, a field of work, a city — and does not put the house of God at the centre of it has stopped short of what the word means.
roots_summary: Hebrew kabash (H3533), to subdue, to bring into bondage — the verb of Genesis 1:28; kana' (H3665), to humble or bring low, used of Moab in Judges 3:30.
roots_lines: Hebrew kabash (H3533) — to subdue; Genesis 1:28, Numbers 32:22, Joshua 18:1.
Hebrew kana' (H3665) — to bring low, subdue; Judges 3:30, of Moab.
Hebrew lipne YHWH — before the LORD; the qualifier Moses attaches to the subduing.
Hebrew nuach (H5117) — to rest; the land had rest fourscore years.
Hebrew 'ohel mo'ed — tabernacle of the congregation; set up as soon as the land was subdued.
usage: “And the land be subdued before the LORD” — the qualifier is the doctrine.
“The land was subdued before them” — and the tabernacle went up at Shiloh.
“So Moab was subdued that day… And the land had rest” — conquest that yields rest.

pos: n. pl. (those who share in a thing; Greek metochos, koinonos)
etymology: From part and take — those who take part. The Greek words behind it mean sharers and fellows, and the New Testament uses them of the highest privileges and the worst complicities alike.
biblical_def: To be a partaker is to have an actual share, not a sympathy. Christ uses the word of a guilt the Pharisees disowned: “If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets” (Mat 23:30) — and He answers that they are building the tombs and finishing the work. Paul uses it of a debt between Jew and Gentile: “For if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, their duty is also to minister unto them in carnal things” (Rom 15:27), and of the minister's right to support: “they which wait at the altar are partakers with the altar” (1Co 9:13). He uses it of the Lord's table: “For we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread” (1Co 10:17). Hebrews stakes assurance on it: “For we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end” (Heb 3:14). And Peter reaches the summit: “that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust” (2Pe 1:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a partaker as one who has or takes a part, share or portion in common with others; an accomplice; an associate.
webster_full: PARTAKER, n. One who has or takes a part, share or portion in common with others; a sharer; as a partaker of the benefits of the gospel.
2. An accomplice; an associate; as a partaker in another's guilt.
PARTAKE, v.i. To take a part, portion or share in common with others.
scriptures: And say, If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partakers with them in the blood of the prophets.
For we being many are one bread, and one body: for we are all partakers of that one bread.
Heb 3:14
For we are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end;
Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust.
corruption_summary: Partaking of the divine nature is read as a promise of deification, while Peter grounds it in escaping corruption and Hebrews conditions it on perseverance.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Peter 1:4 has been made to carry more than it says. Eastern theosis in its stronger forms, and the Word-of-Faith teaching that believers are little gods, both quote the verse and both drop its context. Peter's partaking is by the exceeding great and precious promises, it is defined in the same breath as having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust, and the next verses are a list of virtues to be added with all diligence. The creature does not become the Creator. He is made holy, and holiness is the nature he comes to share.

Hebrews 3:14 supplies the guard on the other side. We are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of our confidence stedfast unto the end. The perfect tense is real — we are made partakers — and the condition is real too. That is perseverance rather than bare eternal security: the holding fast does not earn the share, it evidences it, and Scripture is content to state both without apology.
roots_summary: Greek metochos (G3353), a sharer, partner; koinonos (G2844), a fellow, partaker; sugkoinonos (G4791), joint partaker; the family behind koinonia, fellowship.
roots_lines: Greek metochos (G3353) — partaker, partner; Hebrews 3:14, 12:8.
Greek koinonos (G2844) — partaker, fellow; Matthew 23:30, 1 Corinthians 10:18, 2 Peter 1:4.
Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, communion; the same root.
Greek metecho (G3348) — to partake, to share in; 1 Corinthians 10:17.
Greek phusis (G5449) — nature; the divine nature of 2 Peter 1:4.
usage: “We are all partakers of that one bread” — the table makes one body.
“Partakers of Christ, if we hold… stedfast unto the end” — the share and the holding.
“Partakers with them in the blood of the prophets” — a share nobody claims.

pos: v. (became pregnant; also, formed in the mind or heart; Hebrew harah)
etymology: Latin concipere, to take together, to take in. Scripture uses one family of words for the conceiving of a child and the conceiving of a purpose — both are a thing taken in that will come out.
biblical_def: Conceived is a word Scripture uses at the beginning of lives and of sins. The first human generation: “And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain, and said, I have gotten a man from the LORD” (Gen 4:1). The complication Abram made: “And he went in unto Hagar, and she conceived: and when she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes” (Gen 16:4). The promise kept: “For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him” (Gen 21:2). And the psalmist turns the word on himself in the great confession: Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me — not an accusation against his mother but against the nature he received at conception. James uses the same figure for the birth of sin: when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin. The word carries a claim modern debate resists: that what is conceived is already a somebody with a nature, and that the moral history of a man begins earlier than his memory does.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conceive as to receive into the womb and breed; and, figuratively, to form in the mind; to imagine; to devise.
webster_full: CONCEIVE, v.t. To receive into the womb and breed; to begin the formation of the embryo or fetus.
2. To form in the mind; to imagine; to devise.
3. To comprehend; to understand.
CONCEIVED, pp. Formed in the womb; framed in the mind; devised; understood.
scriptures: Gen 4:1
And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain, and said, I have gotten a man from the LORD.
Gen 16:4
And he went in unto Hagar, and she conceived: and when she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes.
Gen 21:2
For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.
Gen 16:5
And Sarai said unto Abram, My wrong be upon thee: I have given my maid into thy bosom; and when she saw that she had conceived, I was despised in her eyes: the LORD judge between me and thee.
corruption_summary: Conception is treated as the start of a process that only later becomes a person, while Scripture speaks of the conceived child as already bearing a nature and already known to God.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 51:5 places the sinner's nature at conception rather than at birth or at the age of accountability: in sin did my mother conceive me. The verse is a doctrine of original sin, and it carries an anthropology with it — there is a me at conception to have a nature. Psalm 139 says the same from the other side: thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect. A being God is addressing and forming is not a candidate for personhood awaiting a threshold.

The consequence for the defence of unborn life is direct, and it does not depend on sentiment. Scripture does not argue that the unborn child is valuable because it is innocent or wanted; Psalm 51 says the opposite about innocence. It treats the conceived child as a person under God's eye and God's claim from the first, which is why Exodus 21 penalizes harm to the unborn and why Luke reports a baby leaping in the womb at the greeting of a mother six months further along.
roots_summary: Hebrew harah (H2029), to conceive, be with child; yacham (H3179), to conceive or be in heat; Greek sullambano (G4815), to conceive, and kuophoreo, to bear in the womb.
roots_lines: Hebrew harah (H2029) — to conceive; Genesis 4:1, 16:4, 21:2, Psalm 51:5.
Hebrew yacham (H3179) — to conceive; Psalm 51:5, in sin did my mother conceive me.
Greek sullambano (G4815) — to conceive; Luke 1:24, 1:31, 1:36.
Greek kuophoreo — to bear in the womb; the New Testament's language for gestation.
Hebrew golem (H1564) — unformed substance; Psalm 139:16, thine eyes did see my substance.
usage: “And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived” — the first generation.
“Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age” — at the set time God had spoken.
“When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes” — a household ruined.

pos: n. pl. (allotted portions; also, factions in a congregation; Hebrew machaloqeth, Greek dichostasia)
etymology: Latin dividere, to separate. The KJV uses it for two opposite things: the orderly allotments God assigns, and the factions men make.
biblical_def: Divisions in the Old Testament are usually a good order. Joshua allots the land: “So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD said unto Moses; and Joshua gave it for an inheritance unto Israel according to their divisions by their tribes. And the land rested from war” (Josh 11:23), and again, “And Joshua cast lots for them in Shiloh before the LORD: and there Joshua divided the land unto the children of Israel according to their divisions” (Josh 18:10). But Deborah's song already shows the word turning: “For the divisions of Reuben there were great thoughts of heart” (Jdg 5:15), and the refrain sharpens it, “Why abodest thou among the sheepfolds, to hear the bleatings of the flocks? For the divisions of Reuben there were great searchings of heart” (Jdg 5:16). In the New Testament the sense is wholly negative: “that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment” (1Co 1:10), and “mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them” (Rom 16:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines division as the act of dividing; the state of being divided; that which divides; and, in a body of people, discord, disunion, difference in opinion producing separation.
webster_full: DIVISION, n. The act of dividing or separating into parts.
2. The state of being divided.
3. That which divides or separates; a partition.
4. A part or distinct portion; as the divisions of a discourse.
5. Disunion; discord; variance; difference.
scriptures: Josh 11:23

So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD said unto Moses; and Joshua gave it for an inheritance unto Israel according to their divisions by their tribes. And the land rested from war.
Jdg 5:16
Why abodest thou among the sheepfolds, to hear the bleatings of the flocks? For the divisions of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Now I beseech you, brethren, mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them.
corruption_summary: Separation from error is condemned as divisiveness, while Romans 16 makes doctrine the test of who is actually causing the division.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 16:17 supplies the standard that settles most disputes about who is divisive. Paul does not say to mark those who disagree, or those who are difficult, or those who will not go along. He says mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them. The measure is the doctrine already received. A man who separates over the received doctrine is causing division; a man who separates from those who abandon it is obeying this verse.

1 Corinthians 1:10 keeps that from becoming a licence. Paul's remedy for the Corinthian parties — I am of Paul, I of Apollos, I of Cephas — is not that everyone find his preferred teacher and depart in peace, but that they be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment. Judges 5 shows the cost when a tribe declines the summons: for the divisions of Reuben there were great searchings of heart, and Reuben stayed among the sheepfolds while Israel fought.
roots_summary: Hebrew machaloqeth (H4256), a division or course, as of priests and Levites; pelaggah (H6391), a division, in Judges 5; Greek dichostasia (G1370), dissension, and schisma (G4978), a rent.
roots_lines: Hebrew machaloqeth (H4256) — division, course; Joshua 11:23, 18:10, 1 Chronicles 24:1.
Hebrew pelaggah (H6391) — division; Judges 5:15, 5:16, of Reuben.
Greek dichostasia (G1370) — division, sedition; Romans 16:17, Galatians 5:20.
Greek schisma (G4978) — rent, schism; 1 Corinthians 1:10.
Greek didache (G1322) — doctrine; the standard by which divisions are judged.
usage: “According to their divisions by their tribes” — God's allotment, and the land rested.
“For the divisions of Reuben there were great searchings of heart” — and he stayed home.
“Mark them which cause divisions… contrary to the doctrine” — the doctrine is the test.

pos: adj. and n. (chief; first in rank; also, the original sum owed; Hebrew rosh, re'shith)
etymology: Latin principalis, first, chief, from princeps. In the KJV it carries both senses English still has: what ranks first, and the original capital of a debt.
biblical_def: Principal serves two senses in the KJV, and both are exact. It marks the chief or best of a kind: “Take thou also unto thee principal spices, of pure myrrh five hundred shekels, and of sweet cinnamon half so much” (Exo 30:23), the ingredients of the holy anointing oil. It marks rank: “And Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers: and Zabud the son of Nathan was principal officer, and the king's friend” (1Ki 4:5), and “the principal scribe of the host, which mustered the people of the land” (2Ki 25:19), taken by the Babylonians at the fall of Jerusalem. And it carries the financial sense in the law of restitution: “Then they shall confess their sin which they have done: and he shall recompense his trespass with the principal thereof, and add unto it the fifth part thereof, and give it unto him against whom he hath trespassed” (Num 5:7). Above all it names what a man should want most: “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding” (Pro 4:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines principal as chief; highest in rank, character or importance; and, as a noun, a capital sum lent on interest, or the original sum of a debt.
webster_full: PRINCIPAL, a. Chief; highest in rank, character or respectability.
2. Chief; most important or considerable; as the principal reason.
PRINCIPAL, n. A chief or head; one who takes the lead.
2. A capital sum lent on interest, due as a debt or used as a fund; so called as being the head or chief, distinguished from interest or profits.
scriptures: Take thou also unto thee principal spices, of pure myrrh five hundred shekels, and of sweet cinnamon half so much, even two hundred and fifty shekels, and of sweet calamus two hundred and fifty shekels,
Num 5:7

Then they shall confess their sin which they have done: and he shall recompense his trespass with the principal thereof, and add unto it the fifth part thereof, and give it unto him against whom he hath trespassed.
And Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers: and Zabud the son of Nathan was principal officer, and the king's friend:
Pro 4:7
Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding.
corruption_summary: Repentance is treated as a matter of feeling and apology, while Numbers 5 requires the principal restored and a fifth added on top.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 5:7 is one of the most practical verses on repentance in Scripture and one of the least preached. Confession comes first — they shall confess their sin which they have done — and then the principal is restored, and a fifth part added, to the person actually wronged. Not to the temple, not to a general fund, and not in place of the confession. Zacchaeus understood the law and went well past it, and the Lord Jesus called that day salvation come to his house.

The other sense governs Proverbs 4:7, which is the Bible's clearest statement of priority: Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding. The verse assumes a man will be getting things — it does not scold him for it — and it fixes what must be got first. Solomon, who wrote it, asked for exactly that and was given the rest besides, which is the pattern the Lord repeats in Matthew 6: seek ye first the kingdom of God.
roots_summary: Hebrew rosh (H7218), head, chief — both the principal spices and the principal of a debt; re'shith (H7225), beginning, first; chomesh (H2549), the fifth part added in restitution.
roots_lines: Hebrew rosh (H7218) — head, chief, principal; Exodus 30:23, Numbers 5:7.
Hebrew re'shith (H7225) — beginning, chief; Proverbs 4:7, wisdom is the principal thing.
Hebrew chomesh (H2549) — a fifth part; added to the principal in restitution.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; the principal thing to be got.
Hebrew 'asham (H817) — trespass, guilt offering; the setting of the restitution law.
usage: “Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom” — first, not only.
“He shall recompense his trespass with the principal thereof, and add unto it the fifth part” — repentance with a ledger.
“Take thou also unto thee principal spices” — the best of the kind, for the holy oil.

etymology: Latin salvus, safe, whole. The Hebrew betach is built on batach, to trust — in Scripture safety and trust are the same root, because safety is a place you are put, not a thing you build.
biblical_def: Safety in Scripture is covenantal, and it is nearly always tied to dwelling. The law of jubilee promises it as the fruit of obedience: “Wherefore ye shall do my statutes, and keep my judgments, and do them; and ye shall dwell in the land in safety” (Lev 25:18), and “the land shall yield her fruit, and ye shall eat your fill, and dwell therein in safety” (Lev 25:19). Moses promises it of the settled land: “when he giveth you rest from all your enemies round about, so that ye dwell in safety” (Deu 12:10), and blesses Benjamin with it: “The beloved of the LORD shall dwell in safety by him; and the LORD shall cover him all the day long, and he shall dwell between his shoulders” (Deu 33:12). Proverbs locates it in counsel: “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14). Job locates it in God's reversal of fortunes: “To set up on high those that be low; that those which mourn may be exalted to safety” (Job 5:11). And David locates it where the word's root does: “I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety” (Psa 4:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines safety as freedom from danger or hazard; exemption from hurt, injury or loss; preservation from escape.
webster_full: SAFETY, n. Freedom from danger or hazard; as the safety of an army.
2. Exemption from hurt, injury or loss.
3. Preservation from escape; close custody.
SAFE, a. Free from danger of any kind; as safe from enemies.
scriptures: Wherefore ye shall do my statutes, and keep my judgments, and do them; and ye shall dwell in the land in safety.
And of Benjamin he said, The beloved of the LORD shall dwell in safety by him; and the LORD shall cover him all the day long, and he shall dwell between his shoulders.
Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
Psa 4:8
I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
corruption_summary: Safety has become the highest civic and personal value, while Scripture treats it as a gift from God and never as a reason to disobey Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The Hebrew settles the matter of where safety comes from: betach, safety, is the noun of batach, to trust. Psalm 4:8 makes the identity explicit — thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety — and David wrote it while men were saying, Who will shew us any good. Safety in Scripture is not the absence of enemies. It is the presence of a Keeper, and a man can lie down and sleep in it while the danger is still outside.

That ordering is what the present age has inverted. Safety has become the value to which others are subordinated, so that risk itself is treated as a wrong to be eliminated rather than a cost to be weighed. Scripture's men are told to dwell in safety and are also sent into danger; Paul stood in jeopardy every hour, and the Hebrew midwives feared God rather than the king. A safety that requires disobedience is not the thing Leviticus promised. Proverbs 11:14 gives the practical means, and it is corporate: in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
roots_summary: Hebrew betach (H983), safety, security; from batach (H982), to trust; yesha' (H3468), salvation or safety, in Job 5:11 and Proverbs 21:31.
roots_lines: Hebrew betach (H983) — safety, securely; Leviticus 25:18, Deuteronomy 33:12, Psalm 4:8.
Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to be confident; the root of the noun.
Hebrew yesha' (H3468) — safety, salvation; Job 5:11, exalted to safety.
Hebrew teshu'ah (H8668) — deliverance, safety; Proverbs 11:14, in the multitude of counsellors.
Hebrew shakan (H7931) — to dwell; safety in Scripture is nearly always a dwelling.
usage: “Thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety” — and he lay down and slept.
“In the multitude of counsellors there is safety” — a corporate means.
“The beloved of the LORD shall dwell in safety by him” — by Him, not by walls.

pos: n. pl. (men of extraordinary stature; Hebrew nephilim, rephaim)
etymology: Greek gigas, through Latin. The KJV uses giants for two distinct Hebrew words — nephilim in Genesis and Numbers, and rephaim of the pre-Israelite peoples of Canaan and Bashan.
biblical_def: Giants renders two Hebrew words. The first belongs to the days before the flood: “There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown” (Gen 6:4). The second belongs to the conquest, and it is the report that broke Israel's nerve at Kadesh: “And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Num 13:33). Moses records the local names: “Which also were accounted giants, as the Anakims; but the Moabites call them Emims” (Deu 2:11), and “That also was accounted a land of giants: giants dwelt therein in old time; and the Ammonites call them Zamzummims” (Deu 2:20). One survivor is measured: “For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of giants; behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron… nine cubits was the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it” (Deu 3:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a giant as a man of extraordinary bulk and stature; and notes the Scriptural use of a race of men of great size before and after the flood.
webster_full: GIANT, n. A man of extraordinary bulk and stature.
2. A person of extraordinary strength or powers, bodily or intellectual.
GIANTLY, a. Giantlike; bulky.
GIGANTIC, a. Of extraordinary size; very large; huge.
scriptures: Gen 6:4

There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.
And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.
Deu 2:11
Which also were accounted giants, as the Anakims; but the Moabites call them Emims.
Deu 3:11

For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of giants; behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron; is it not in Rabbath of the children of Ammon? nine cubits was the length thereof, and four cubits the breadth of it, after the cubit of a man.
corruption_summary: The giants are handled either as mythology to be discarded or as a doorway into speculation Scripture does not open; the text treats them as men, measured and defeated.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern academic reading files Genesis 6:4 under legendary material and moves on, which is not an interpretation but an evasion; Moses records the giants in the same register as the genealogies around them, and Numbers and Deuteronomy treat them as an ordinary military problem with local names attached. The opposite error is now more common in popular teaching, where the sons of God and their offspring have become the subject of elaborate systems the text does not sustain. Scripture gives a short account, tells us what the LORD did about it, and does not gratify curiosity.

What the passages do press is the failure at Kadesh. Ten spies saw the giants and said, we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight — and note that the second half was a guess. They had no way of knowing how they looked to the Anakim, and Rahab later reports that Jericho had been terrified of Israel for forty years. Unbelief measures itself against the obstacle and then invents the obstacle's opinion of it. Deuteronomy 3:11 is the LORD's answer: the last of the giants is a bedstead in a museum.
roots_summary: Hebrew nephilim (H5303), the fallen ones, in Genesis 6:4 and Numbers 13:33; rephaim (H7497), the giant peoples of Canaan and Bashan; 'Anaq (H6061), Anak.
roots_lines: Hebrew nephilim (H5303) — giants; Genesis 6:4, Numbers 13:33.
Hebrew rephaim (H7497) — giants, the ancient peoples; Deuteronomy 2:11, 3:11.
Hebrew 'Anaq (H6061) — Anak; the sons of Anak seen at Hebron.
Hebrew 'Emim (H368) and Zamzummim (H2157) — the Moabite and Ammonite names for them.
Hebrew gibborim (H1368) — mighty men; the same verse, men of renown.
usage: “There were giants in the earth in those days” — reported, not explained.
“We were in our own sight as grasshoppers” — and the second half was a guess.
“Only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of giants” — and his bed was on display.

pos: n. and v. (a whip; a sweeping affliction; Hebrew shot, Greek mastix)
etymology: Old French escorgier, to whip, from Latin excoriare, to flay. Scripture uses it of the lash, of a devastating calamity, and of the Father's discipline of His sons.
biblical_def: Scourge runs from the literal whip to the sweep of judgment. Job knows both a spoken lash and a sudden one: “Thou shalt be hid from the scourge of the tongue: neither shalt thou be afraid of destruction when it cometh” (Job 5:21); “If the scourge slay suddenly, he will laugh at the trial of the innocent” (Job 9:23). Isaiah uses it of the LORD raising an instrument against Assyria: “And the LORD of hosts shall stir up a scourge for him according to the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb” (Isa 10:26). And in the great oracle against the scoffers of Jerusalem, the word names the coming disaster twice, once in their boast and once in God's answer: “when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us: for we have made lies our refuge” (Isa 28:15), and “when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, then ye shall be trodden down by it” (Isa 28:18). The New Testament makes the word intimate: “For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth” (Heb 12:6). Christ Himself was scourged before He was crucified.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a scourge as a whip; a lash consisting of a strap or cord; and figuratively, a punishment, or a means of inflicting punishment or affliction.
webster_full: SCOURGE, n. A whip; a lash consisting of a strap or cord; an instrument of punishment or discipline.
2. A punishment; vindictive affliction.
3. He or that which greatly afflicts, harasses or destroys; particularly, any continued evil or calamity.
SCOURGE, v.t. To whip severely; to lash.
2. To punish with severity; to chastise; to afflict for sins or faults.
scriptures: Job 5:21
Thou shalt be hid from the scourge of the tongue: neither shalt thou be afraid of destruction when it cometh.

Because ye have said, We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us: for we have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves:
And your covenant with death shall be disannulled, and your agreement with hell shall not stand; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, then ye shall be trodden down by it.
Heb 12:6
For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.
corruption_summary: The chastening of God is treated as inconsistent with His love, while Hebrews makes it the evidence of sonship and the absence of it the mark of a bastard.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 12:6 puts the hardest word in the New Testament beside the tenderest: whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. The next verses press it further — if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons. The modern instinct is to protect God's reputation by denying that He sends the hard thing. Hebrews does the opposite: it protects the believer's assurance by insisting He does, and by naming the scourge as proof of the relation rather than a threat to it.

Isaiah 28 shows the alternative to being scourged as a son. The rulers of Jerusalem had made a covenant with death and told themselves the overflowing scourge would pass by; the LORD answers that the covenant shall be disannulled, and adds that the bed is shorter than a man can stretch himself on it. A refuge of lies keeps out nothing. The choice Scripture offers is not between the scourge and safety, but between the Father's discipline and the flood.
roots_summary: Hebrew shot (H7752), a whip or scourge; Greek mastix (G3148), a scourge or plague; mastigoo (G3146), to scourge, in Hebrews 12:6; phragelloo (G5417), the Roman flogging of Christ.
roots_lines: Hebrew shot (H7752) — scourge, whip; Job 5:21, Isaiah 10:26, 28:15.
Greek mastigoo (G3146) — to scourge; Hebrews 12:6, of every son received.
Greek mastix (G3148) — scourge, plague; Mark 3:10, of diseases.
Greek phragelloo (G5417) — to flog with the Roman scourge; Matthew 27:26, Mark 15:15.
Greek paideuo (G3811) — to chasten, to train a child; the verb paired with scourging in Hebrews 12:6.
usage: “The scourge of the tongue” — a lash that leaves no mark.
“When the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us” — the boast God disannuls.
“Scourgeth every son whom he receiveth” — the evidence, not the exception.

pos: n. pl. (women who assist at birth; Hebrew meyalledeth)
etymology: Middle English midwif, literally with-woman — she who is with the mother. The Hebrew is a participle of yalad, to bear, so the Hebrew names them by the act they assist.
biblical_def: The midwives of Exodus 1 are the first recorded case of civil disobedience in Scripture, and God commends them by name. “And the king of Egypt spake to the Hebrew midwives, of which the name of the one was Shiphrah, and the name of the other Puah” (Exo 1:15). The order was infanticide. Their answer was silence and sabotage: “But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive” (Exo 1:17). Summoned to account, they gave Pharaoh an explanation he could not check: “And the king of Egypt called for the midwives, and said unto them, Why have ye done this thing, and have saved the men children alive?” (Exo 1:18); “And the midwives said unto Pharaoh, Because the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women; for they are lively, and are delivered ere the midwives come in unto them” (Exo 1:19). And the verdict follows immediately: “Therefore God dealt well with the midwives: and the people multiplied, and waxed very mighty” (Exo 1:20), and the next verse says He made them houses.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a midwife as a woman who assists other women in childbirth; and midwifery as the art or practice of assisting women in parturition.
webster_full: MIDWIFE, n. A woman who assists other women in childbirth.
MIDWIFERY, n. The art or practice of assisting women in childbirth; obstetrics.
2. Assistance at childbirth; help or co-operation in production.
scriptures: Exo 1:15
And the king of Egypt spake to the Hebrew midwives, of which the name of the one was Shiphrah, and the name of the other Puah:
Exo 1:17
But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive.
Exo 1:19
And the midwives said unto Pharaoh, Because the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women; for they are lively, and are delivered ere the midwives come in unto them.
Exo 1:20
Therefore God dealt well with the midwives: and the people multiplied, and waxed very mighty.
corruption_summary: Obedience to the state is treated as the Christian default, while Exodus 1 records two women defying a royal decree and God building them houses for it.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 1 establishes the limit of civil authority before Israel is even a nation. The magistrate commanded the killing of infants; the midwives feared God and refused; and the narrative does not present this as a tragic dilemma but as obedience. Romans 13 is not thereby overturned — the powers that be are ordained of God — but Acts 5:29 states the boundary the midwives had already kept: we ought to obey God rather than men. A ruler commanding what God forbids has stepped outside the authority he was given.

Two further details deserve notice. The first is that Scripture preserves the names, Shiphrah and Puah, while never naming the Pharaoh they defied. The second is what God gave them: he made them houses — households, descendants. Women who refused to destroy children were given children. Exodus 1:20 says the people multiplied and waxed very mighty in the same breath, and the deliverer of that nation was born a chapter later to a mother who hid him three months.
roots_summary: Hebrew meyalledeth (H3205), midwife, from yalad, to bear or bring forth; Shiphrah (H8236), beauty; Pu'ah (H6326), splendour; yare' (H3372), to fear.
roots_lines: Hebrew yalad (H3205) — to bear, bring forth; the participle rendered midwife.
Hebrew Shiphrah (H8236) — Shiphrah, beauty; the first midwife named.
Hebrew Pu'ah (H6326) — Puah; the second, named beside her.
Hebrew yare' 'elohim — feared God; the stated reason for their refusal.
Hebrew bayith (H1004) — house; he made them houses, Exodus 1:21.
usage: “But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them” — the whole doctrine.
“Therefore God dealt well with the midwives” — the verdict, plainly given.
Scripture keeps their names and withholds Pharaoh's.

pos: n. pl. (those driven out; the banished of Israel; Hebrew nadach)
etymology: From out and cast — those thrown out. The Hebrew participle niddach means driven away or banished, and in the prophets it is almost a technical term for the scattered of the covenant people.
biblical_def: Outcasts in Scripture are the driven-away of God's people, and He never speaks of them as lost. The psalmist joins the word to the building of the city: “The LORD doth build up Jerusalem: he gathereth together the outcasts of Israel” (Psa 147:2). Isaiah makes their gathering the work of the messianic ensign: “And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth” (Isa 11:12), and again at the trumpet: “they shall come which were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and the outcasts in the land of Egypt, and shall worship the LORD in the holy mount at Jerusalem” (Isa 27:13). He also commands a nation to shelter them: “Take counsel, execute judgment… hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth” (Isa 16:3), and “Let mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab; be thou a covert to them from the face of the spoiler” (Isa 16:4). Note the possessive: mine outcasts. And Jeremiah records what the nations called Zion and what the LORD answered: “because they called thee an Outcast, saying, This is Zion, whom no man seeketh after” (Jer 30:17) — and the same verse begins, I will restore health unto thee.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an outcast as one who is cast out or expelled; an exile; one driven from home or country; and, in Scripture, a person rejected of men.
webster_full: OUTCAST, pp. Cast out; thrown away; rejected as useless.
OUTCAST, n. One who is cast out or expelled; an exile; one driven from home or country.
2. In Scripture, one banished or driven away, but not forgotten of God.
scriptures: The LORD doth build up Jerusalem: he gathereth together the outcasts of Israel.
And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
Isa 16:4
Let mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab; be thou a covert to them from the face of the spoiler: for the extortioner is at an end, the spoiler ceaseth, the oppressors are consumed out of the land.
For I will restore health unto thee, and I will heal thee of thy wounds, saith the LORD; because they called thee an Outcast, saying, This is Zion, whom no man seeketh after.
corruption_summary: The marginalized are made an autonomous political category, while Scripture calls the driven-away God's own and holds their scattering to be His judgment and their gathering His work.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture has a great deal to say about the driven-away, and none of it fits the modern category of the marginalized as an identity that confers moral standing. Isaiah's outcasts are outcasts because God scattered them for covenant-breaking; they remain mine outcasts while scattered; and their gathering is accomplished by an ensign lifted up for the nations, not by their own assertion. The biblical categories are the exile, the stranger, the widow, the fatherless and the afflicted, and each of them is defined by what God says and does, not by a position in a social hierarchy.

What Scripture does demand is concrete and costly. Isaiah 16 orders Moab — a hostile nation — to hide the outcasts, to be a covert to them from the face of the spoiler, and not to betray the one who wanders. That is a command to shelter refugees of a people not one's own, issued to a nation under judgment, and the chapter goes on to pronounce Moab's doom partly for pride. The church that will not shelter the driven-away has failed a test that was once set for Moab.
roots_summary: Hebrew nadach (H5080), to drive away, banish; the passive participle niddach is the prophets' word for the outcasts; qabats (H6908), to gather, is always the answer to it.
roots_lines: Hebrew nadach (H5080) — to drive out, banish; Isaiah 11:12, 16:3, 27:13.
Hebrew qabats (H6908) — to gather; Psalm 147:2, he gathereth together the outcasts.
Hebrew nes (H5251) — ensign, banner; lifted for the nations, Isaiah 11:12.
Hebrew sether (H5643) — covert, hiding place; be thou a covert to them, Isaiah 16:4.
Hebrew 'arukah (H724) — healing, restoration; I will restore health unto thee, Jeremiah 30:17.
usage: “He gathereth together the outcasts of Israel” — in the same verse as building the city.
“Let mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab” — and the possessive is the point.
“They called thee an Outcast… I will restore health unto thee” — the world's name, God's answer.
